Effective pretreatment of tea stem via poly-deep eutectic solvent for promoting platform molecule production and obtaining fluorescent lignin
Pei-Ru Zhouª, Xiao-Ping Zhengª, Ya-Peng Duª, Yu Chaiª, Yu-Cang Zhangª,ᵇ,ᶜ, Yan-Zhen Zhengª,ᵇ,ᶜ,*

a College of Ocean Food and Biological Engineering, Jimei University, Xiamen 361021, China b Fujian Provincial Key Laboratory of Food Microbiology and Enzyme Engineering, Xiamen 361021, China c Research center of food biotechnology of Xiamen city, Xiamen, Fujian 361021, China
ARTICLE INFO --- Keywords: Lignocellulose Poly-deep eutectic solvents Pretreatment

ABSTRACT In this study, polyethylene glycol 200 (PEG200) was employed as hydrogen bond acceptor, while organic acids served as hydrogen bond donors, to formulate poly-deep eutectic solvents (PDESs), which were utilized to pretreat tea stem. Specially, combining PEG200 and oxalic acid (OA) exhibited a notably high cellulose retention (82.03%) and most efficient hemicellulose (97.02%) and lignin removal (70.89%). The removal of amorphous lignin enhanced the crystallinity of the residues and improved the conversion efficiency of cellulose into levulinic acid. Additionally, the structural alterations in lignin samples were analyzed in comparison to milled wood lignin (MWL). The PEG200-OA system facilitated the cleavage of β-O-4 and β-5 linkages and resulted in the degradation of S-type lignin, accompanied by increased condensation of G units. The resulting lignin displayed a reduced molecular weight (Mw of 1283 g/mol, Mn value 531 g/mol) and nanoscale particle size (D50 212 nm). Furthermore, fluorescent lignin was synthesized through simple oxidation and was used to detect metal ions. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations supported that both PEG200 and OA played a significant role in lignin dissolution, with the weak interactions between DES and lignin primarily driven by hydrogen bonding (characterized as weak, closed-shell, and electrostatic) and van der Waals forces.

## 1. Introduction As global fossil fuel reserves dwindle and environmental challenges intensify, the role of bio-refinery technology in efficiently converting lignocellulosic biomass into energy and chemicals becomes increasingly important. Lignocellulose primarily consists of hemicellulose (23% to 32%), cellulose (38% to 50%), and lignin (15% to 25%) [1]. Hemi-cellulose and cellulose can be hydrolyzed or pyrolyzed to produce various biofuels and biochemicals, including monosaccharides like mannose, glucose, and arabinose [2,3]. Lignin, a complex and amorphous polymer, is derived from phenylpropane units and features a variety of hydrophilic functional groups such as carboxylic acids and hydroxyl groups [4]. This unique structure allows lignin to be used in the production of lignin-based nanoparticles, flocculants, and luminescent materials, among other applications [5-7]. However, the intricate network of covalent and hydrogen bonds linking cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin poses significant challenges for biomass utilization [8]. Pretreatment of lignocellulose is a crucial step in improving its usability

and sustainability [9]. This process alters the biomass's structural com- ponents, making it more amenable to conversion into valuable products while reducing waste and meeting the growing demand for high-value commodities [9].

Various pretreatment methods, such as alkaline treatments and organic solvent applications, have been developed to enhance this transformation [10]. However, traditional pretreatment methods often face significant challenges, including equipment corrosion, volatility issues, and the requirement for extreme conditions, all of which pose operational risks and can diminish profitability [11]. Additionally, during many pretreatment processes, lignin is prone to depolymerization and condensation, complicating its recovery and subsequent use. Therefore, the development of more efficient and environmentally friendly pretreatment strategies is crucial for optimizing the economic and ecological benefits of lignocellulose utilization [11].

Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) are gaining great attention as prom- ising, eco-friendly alternatives to traditional solvents for the fraction- ation of biomass components [12,13]. Notable for their simple synthesis,

The formation of a network of hydrogen bonds between a hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA) and a hydrogen bond donor (HBD) enhances the dissolution and separation of biomass components [14]. In the pretreatment of ligno-cellulosic biomass, DESs have shown a remarkable ability to disrupt the lignin-carbohydrate complex (LCC) and improve lignin dissolution [13,15,16]. This effectiveness has led to the exploration of various DES formulations to overcome biomass recalcitrance in bioenergy production. Additionally, reactive DESs offer the advantage of introducing functional groups such as carbonyl, carboxylic, and ammonium groups during pretreatment [15]. This dual functionality can reduce the need for additional chemicals and energy inputs, presenting a more sustain-able approach to biomass conversion.

China is the world's largest producer and consumer of tea. The deep processing of tea into products like tea beverages, instant tea, and tea polyphenols generates substantial amounts of tea stem [17,18]. Disposing of this residue as waste not only squanders valuable resources but also poses environmental risks, contributing to pollution and ecological damage. Tea stem is primarily composed of cellulose, hemi-cellulose and lignin. Currently, the focus of tea stem utilization in China is largely on extracting active compounds such as tea polyphenols and tea polysaccharides [19]. However, the potential value-added applica-tions of lignin, hemicellulose, and cellulose from tea stem remain largely underexplored. Therefore, pretreating tea stem to effectively separate cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin is crucial for the sustainable utili-zation of tea stem resources, offering significant environmental and economic benefits. DESs have been used for the pretreatment of multiple lignocelluloses [20,21], however, there remains a significant opportu-nity to derive greater value from the extracted fractions of tea stem. Besides, beyond the conversion of carbohydrates into biofuels and bio-chemicals, further utilization of lignin could enhance both the economic viability and environmental sustainability of lignocellulose-based bio-refineries [20,21].

In our study, we present a novel approach for converting tea stem into high-value products. We utilized PDESs composed of PEG200 and OA as an innovative reactive medium for breaking down tea stem, enabling the selective separation of lignocellulosic components. PEG200 serves as a hydrogen bond acceptor and is known for its low viscosity and ability to dissolve a wide range of biomass components, making it an ideal candidate for biomass pretreatment. Organic acids, such as oxalic acid, are efficient hydrogen bond donors, which facilitate the formation of stable DES with PEG200. This specific combination has been shown to enhance the solubility and disrupt the structural integrity of lignocel- lulosic materials, promoting better pretreatment efficiency. Through various analytical techniques, we assessed the impact of PDES treatment on the biomass structure, confirming its effectiveness in selective delignification and hemicellulose removal. We further enhanced the value of the cellulosic fraction by converting it into levulinic acid (LA), one of the top ten pivotal platform chemicals identified by the U.S. Department of Energy, thus maximizing the utility of cellulose derived from tea stem [22]. This conversion process not only increased the economic potential of the biomass but also confirmed the pretreatment method enhanced cellulose digestibility. The recovered lignin was thoroughly characterized, including analyses of molecular weight, par- ticle size, and structural properties, with comparisons drawn to milled wood lignin (MWL) to underscore the unique attributes resulting from our process. Moreover, the application of the recovered lignin was explored by synthesizing fluorescent lignin via a simple method, which was successfully utilized in detecting Fe3+ ions, opening new possibil- ities for lignin use. Furthermore, density functional theory (DFT) cal- culations were employed, with the combination of the experimental results to provide a comprehensive understanding of the mechanisms driving efficient lignin extraction. Overall, this study introduced the PDES system composed of PEG200 and oxalic acid for efficiently

breaking down tea stem, enabling selective lignocellulose separation and high-value conversion of cellulose into levulinic acid. Additionally, the recovered lignin was valorized as a fluorescent material for Fe3+ detection, and DFT analysis provided new insights into the extraction mechanisms, showcasing a sustainable and integrated approach for agricultural byproduct utilization.

## 2. Materials and methods ### 2.1. Materials Tea stem, obtained from a local vendor in Xiamen, China, were first rinsed with deionized water and then subjected to thermal drying at 80 °C to eliminate moisture. After drying, the material was mechanically ground and passed through an 80-mesh sieve to produce a consistent, fine tea stem powder. This powder was directly used in subsequent experiments without further modification. PEG200 was purchased from Aladdin Reagent Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China. Various organic acids, including levulinic acid, oxalic acid, formic acid, and lactic acid, were sourced from Rhawn Reagent Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China. Additionally, the catalyst 1-sulfobutyl-3-methylimidazole p-toluenesulfonate ([C4SO3Hmim][PhSO3]), with a purity of over 99%, was supplied by Shanghai Cheng Jie Chemical Co., Ltd. Other analytical-grade chemicals were procured from Aladdin Reagent Co., Ltd.

2.2. Preparation of deep eutectic solvent The selected organic acids and PEG200 were mixed in 1:2 M ratio and blended under vigorous stirring at 80 °C, resulting in the formation of translucent DES. After cooling to room temperature, the solution remained clear and uniform, confirming the successful synthesis of the DESs. Using a similar approach, a series of PEG200-OA DESs, varying the molar ratios of HBA/HBD, was prepared.

Lignin, a complex phenolic polymer composed of the three primary alcohol monomers: p-coumaryl alcohol, coniferyl alcohol, and sinapyl alcohol, presents substantial challenges for structural simulation due to its intricate nature. Existing literature widely applied biomass monomers to do the DFT calculations [27,28]. In our study, p-coumaryl alcohol, coniferyl alcohol, and sinapyl alcohol were chosen as representative lignin monomers for DFT analysis. To obtain the geometric structures of PDES-lignin interaction complexes, DFT calculations were conducted using the Gaussian 16 software package [29] based on the M062X/6-311 g(d,p) method. The energy minima of these optimized complexes were confirmed by ensuring that no imaginary frequencies were present, indicating stable configurations. Visualization of the reduced density gradient (RDG) for the interaction complexes was performed with VMD 1.9.4, which utilized data generated by Multiwfn 3.8 [30,31]. Simultaneously, a detailed analysis of atomic interactions within the molecules was carried out based on the atoms in molecules (AIM) theory [32]. Key properties, including electron density (p), the Laplacian of electron density (∇²p), and energy density (H) at the bond critical point (BCP), were derived from the Multiwfn 3.8 output, providing valuable insights into the nature of the intermolecular interactions.

## 3. Results and discussion ### 3.1. Delignification efficiency by deep eutectic solvent The pretreatment experiments were conducted using a mixture of HBA (PEG200) and HBD (organic acid) at a molar ratio of 2:1, under a temperature of 100 °C for 3 h. All the Brønsted acid-type HBD tested (levulinic acid, oxalic acid, formic acid, and lactic acid) were able to form homogenous PDES with PEG200. The results indicated that PEG200-based Brønsted acid PDESs were effective in delignifying tea stem, achieving successful removal of lignin and hemicellulose. In this process, lignin was extracted into the PDES, while the hemicellulose was removed primarily due to the conversion into valuable intermediates such as furfural and LA under acidic conditions. Among the PDESs, PEG200-OA exhibited the highest delignification efficiency (40.49%), effectively dissolving lignin while retaining most of the cellulose. This efficiency can be attributed to the ample acid sites and appropriate acidity of the PEG200-OA PDES, which facilitated lignin dissolution and hemicellulose degradation. Besides, PEG200, as a hydrogen bond donor, has low viscosity and excellent solvent properties, allowing it to effectively dissolve various biomass components. Oxalic acid, serving as a hydrogen bond acceptor, helps to form a stable DES with PEG200, enhancing the solubility of lignocellulosic materials. This combination could disrupt the structural integrity of lignocellulose by weakening hydrogen bonds, facilitating the selective separation of lignin and hemicellulose. Consequently, PEG200-OA was selected as the optimal DES for subsequent experiments.

Lignin, an amorphous polymer composed of methoxylated phenyl-propane units linked with phenolic groups [33], was known for emitting strong fluorescence across the visible and far-infrared spectra [34]. It was hypothesized that the fluorescence emitted by lignin in a solvent can serve as an indicator of its dissolution state, which correlated with the deconstruction of tea stem and the material's decrystallization [34]. To investigate this, fluorescence microscopy was employed to monitor lignin's dissolution dynamics in the different PDES systems, as depicted in Fig. 1B. Initially, intense fluorescence was observed in the tea stem solids, with no fluorescence detected in the solvent phase, indicating that lignin was densely encapsulating the tea stem solids. As the disso-lution progressed in the various PDES systems, fluorescence began to appear in the solution, demonstrating effective lignin removal. The PEG200-OA system exhibited significantly higher fluorescence intensity in the solution compared to other systems, indicating greater lignin extraction. Thus, tracking fluorescence intensity within the mixture proved to be a reliable method for monitoring tea stem dissolution and highlighted the superior lignin extraction capability of the PEG200-OA treatment.

## 3.2. Optimization of experimental conditions To achieve optimal efficiency during the PEG200-OA PDES pre-treatment, several key parameters, including reaction temperature, duration, the molar ratio of HBA to HBD, and water content were optimized. Among these, reaction temperature and duration emerged as critical factors influencing the pretreatment outcome. As depicted in Fig. 2A and B, the retention of cellulose within the substrate fluctuated with the reaction temperature, reaching its peak at 120 °C as the tem-perature increased from 100 °C to 150 °C. Hemicellulose removal exceeded 90% when temperatures surpassed 130 °C, likely due to enhanced solvent-induced breakdown of tea stem components at elevated temperatures [37]. The lignin removal rate also rose signifi-cantly with increasing temperature, stabilizing beyond 140 °C. This stabilization could be attributed to the formation of pseudolignin, resulting from the recombination of small molecular fragments in an acidic environment as temperatures rise [38,39]. Considering the composition of the cellulose-rich substrate, the lignin removal rate, and energy consumption, a pretreatment temperature of 140 °C was deemed optimal. This temperature balanced low energy requirements with the highest observed lignin removal rate.

Fig. 2B further illustrated that a 4-h pretreatment duration resulted in a lignin removal rate of 58.30 %. However, extending the pretreat- ment time beyond this point led to a notable decline in lignin removal efficiency, possibly due to pseudolignin formation from tea stem [38,39]. Hemicellulose removal continued to increase up to 4 h, after which it plateaued. The ongoing degradation of hemicellulose during this period can impact the recovery and reuse of the solvent system. The Influence of PDES components, specifically the varying molar ratios of PEG200 to OA, on lignin fractionation efficiency was systematically explored. Fig. 2C highlighted that pure OA struggled to mix effectively with the substrate, rendering it ineffective for pretreating tea stem. Conversely, pure PEG200 exhibited a high cellulose retention rate but demonstrated limited efficiency in lignin removal. As OA was introduced into the mixture, the cellulose retention rate decreased while the hemicellulose removal rate increased, a result of the conversion processes occurring in the acidic environment. Adjusting the PEG200 to OA ratios from 1:1 to 4:1 led to a reduction in delignification efficiency, dropping from 59.11 % to 45.80 %. This result indicated a synergistic interaction between PEG200 and the Brønsted acid present. The Brønsted acid, consisting of small ions, enhanced the swelling of tea stem biomass, thereby improving the PDES's access to lignin-carbohydrate complexes (LCCs). Additionally, the PEG200 stabilized the PDES system by modulating its acidity. However, when the PEG200 content was reduced to a 1:1 ratio with OA, the system's stability was compromised, and PDES formation was ineffective. Thus, a PEG200 to OA molar ratio of 2:1 was identified as the optimal balance, ensuring efficient lignin removal, minimal tea cellulose loss, and a stable PDES solvent system. Beyond the molar ratio, water content also played a critical role in the efficiency of the pretreatment process. Introducing water reduced

the system's viscosity, enhancing the interaction between the substrate and solvent and improving mixture uniformity, which also helped to lower costs. However, it was crucial to consider that water addition may dilute the PDES concentration. As shown in Fig. 2D, the pretreatment efficiency was significantly affected by water content. Hemicellulose and lignin removal rates increased when water content reached 10%, while further increases in water content did not significantly alter cel- lulose retention or hemicellulose removal. The lignin removal rate peaked at 20% water content. Consequently, for both cost-effectiveness and process simplicity, a water content of 20 % was chosen.

In summary, the optimal conditions for the pretreatment process were identified as a temperature of 140 °C, a duration of 4 h, a water content of 20 %, and a PEG200 to OA molar ratio of 2:1. Under these conditions, 82.03 % of cellulose was retained in the solid residues, with 97.02 % of hemicellulose and 70.89 % of lignin successfully removed from the tea stem.

The peak at 1234 cm⁻¹, corresponding to the C—O stretching vibration within ester linkages between lignin and hemicellulose [40–42], disappeared following treatment. This disappearance indicated the removal of hemicellulose and lignin from the tea stem during PEG200-OA pretreatment. After pretreatment, there was a marked increase in the intensity of peaks at 1420 cm⁻¹, 1369 cm⁻¹, 1319 cm⁻¹, 1159 cm⁻¹, 1053 cm⁻¹, and 1028 cm⁻¹, which corresponded to various vibrations such as C—O—C stretching, C—H2 deformation, C—H2 rocking, C—O—C glycoside ether, C—O pyranose ring stretching, and C—O stretching of a primary alcohol [40–42], all of which were characteristic of cellulose in carbohydrates. The distinct band at around 895 cm⁻¹ was attributed to the stretching vibrations of C—O—C, signifying the presence of β-glycosidic bonds within cellulose [40–42]. The enhanced of these bands after treatment indicated the enrichment of cellulose in the solid residues. In the untreated tea stem, a spectral band around 1731 cm⁻¹, indicative of carbonyl groups (C=O), was observed in both lignin and hemicellulose [40–42]. The persistence of this band in the cellulose-rich solid residue suggested that carbonyl stretching vibrations, primarily due to the esterification of OA with cellulose hydroxyl groups, remained present post-treatment.

Fig. 3B showed the XRD patterns of both untreated tea stem and cellulose-rich residue. After treatment, the solid residues showed increased peak intensity at 16.5° and 34.5°, indicative of a strengthened cellulose I structure for the (004) and (110) lattice planes [43,44]. The cellulose crystalline structure remained intact, retaining its cellulose I form post-treatment, suggesting that PEG200-OA primarily acted on lignin and hemicellulose without affecting cellulose crystallinity. The crystallinity index (CrI) was calculated for each sample, revealing a notable increase in the crystallinity of the solid residues after treatment. This increase was likely due to the removal of amorphous components, such as lignin and hemicellulose, during the pretreatment process [45]. These results align with previous studies that had demonstrated an increase in crystallinity following lignin and hemicellulose removal through pretreatment.

3.3.2. Utilization of the cellulose-rich solid residues Extensive research had been dedicated to transforming biomass into valuable intermediates, with particular emphasis on LA due to its versatility and potential applications. As lignin is a highly recalcitrant polymer, its presence in the biomass matrix significantly hinders the accessibility of cellulose to catalytic action, thus reducing the efficiency of cellulose conversion. Lignin removal helps to disrupt the biomass structure, improving the porosity and accessibility of cellulose, which in

turn enhances its conversion to levulinic acid. In this study, we effec- tively removed lignin during the pretreatment process. As illustrated in Fig. 3B, LA production markedly increased from 35.7% to 51.5% following PEG200-OA pretreatment. Thus, pretreating tea stem with PEG200-OA significantly enhanced the conversion of cellulose into LA, optimizing the overall process.

Therefore, the PEG200-OA pretreatment successfully removed lignin and hemicellulose without compromising the integrity of the cellulose structure. The elimination of amorphous lignin led to an increase in the crystallinity of the residue, thereby improving the efficiency of cellulose conversion into LA.

3.4.2. Photoluminescence properties and applications of fluorescent lignin The fluorescent lignin was simply prepared via oxidized regenerated lignin by the H2O2 solution. The fluorescent lignin solution was found to have an excitation wavelength around 340 nm (Fig. 6A), with an emission wavelength near 450 nm when excited at 340 nm (Fig. 6B). Under UV light at 365 nm (inset of Fig. 6B), the lignin exhibited strong photoluminescence, emitting a bright fluorescence that indicated good dispersion and uniformity, making it suitable for various applications.

Comparison between the fluorescent lignin prepared from the re- generated lignin and that prepared from MWL was also conducted. The results were present in Fig. S1 in Supporting Information. The fluores- cent lignin derived from regenerated lignin exhibited significantly higher fluorescence intensity than the fluorescent lignin obtained from MWL. This observation highlighted the distinct advantages of the re- generated lignin from PDES in terms of its photoluminescence proper- ties, which could offer improved performance for applications in fluorescence-based sensing or detection.

Heavy metal ions pose significant environmental and health risks, making the development of sensing technologies for detecting these ions crucial. Due to the high quenching effect of heavy metal ions, fluorescent lignin had demonstrated excellent detection capabilities for various

metal ions [49,50]. The influence of the pH on the fluorescence intensity was tested before metal ions detection. In Fig. S2 (Supporting information), as the pH increased, the fluorescence intensity initially increased and then decreased, with the maximum fluorescence intensity observed at pH = 6. This finding highlighted the significant influence of pH on the Fe3+ detection process, which may be attributed to changes in the interaction between Fe3+ ions and the fluorescence probe as well as the protonation state of the probe itself. On the other hand, when the pH value changed from 4 to 7, the fluorescence intensity of the fluorescent lignin was only minimally affected. The pH values of various metal ions also felt within this range, so their impact on subsequent metal ion detection was negligible. As shown in Fig. 6C, the fluorescent lignin solution was tested against different metal ions. The addition of Fe3+ resulted in the most pronounced fluorescence quenching, while other metal ions did not cause significant changes in fluorescence intensity, suggesting that the prepared fluorescent lignin was particularly effective as a probe for detecting iron ions.

3.5. Calculation and analysis of intermolecular interaction by DFT In the previous section, the PEG200-OA PDES system demonstrated considerable effectiveness in lignocellulose pretreatment, particularly in its ability to dissolve lignin. This effectiveness was closely related to the interaction between the PDES components and lignin. To better understand the mechanisms underlying lignin dissolution, we conducted DFT calculations to analyze the interactions between the PEG200-OA system and lignin [51,52]. The geometries of the interaction complexes between PEG200-OA and p-coumaryl alcohol, coniferyl alcohol, and sinapyl alcohol were optimized, with the most stable structures shown in Fig. 7.

2- Fig. 7 illustrated the weak intermolecular interactions identified using the RDG function isosurface (top) and scatter diagram (bottom). Based on the Sign (λ²)p values, these interactions were categorized into hydrogen bonds (blue), van der Waals forces (green), and steric effects (red) [31]. Our analysis revealed that hydrogen bonds and van der Waals forces were the primary interactions between PEG200-OA and

lignin, with both the HBA and HBD playing a synergistic role in lignin removal. Notably, the hydrogen bonds in the PEG200-OA-lignin com- plex were formed between the hydrogen atom on the carboxyl group of the HBD (OA) and the oxygen atom on the alkyl hydroxyl group of lignin.

The properties of these hydrogen bonds were further elucidated through topological analysis using AIM theory, as summarized in Fig. 7. It was found that the ρ at the BCP of a hydrogen bond typically ranged from 0.002 to 0.035 au, while the ∇²ρ at the BCP of non-covalent in- teractions, such as hydrogen bonds, generally fell within the range of 0.024 to 0.139 au. The values of ρ and ∇²ρ for the hydrogen bonds between PEG200 and OA fell within these ranges, confirming the for- mation of hydrogen bonds.

According to established theories [32,53], the strength and nature of hydrogen bonds can be determined by specific criteria. If both the ∇²ρ and the H were negative, the hydrogen bond is considered strong, shared, and covalently dominant. Conversely, if ∇²ρ was positive and H was negative, the bond was of medium strength, closed-shell, and covalently dominant. In cases where both ∇²ρ and H are positive, the hydrogen bond was classified as weak, closed-shell, and electrostatic dominant. In our study, the positive values of ∇²ρ and H indicated that the interactions between PEG200-OA and lignin were weak, closed-shell, and electrostatic in nature.

Specially, combining PEG200 and oxalic acid (OA) exhibited a notably high cellulose retention (82.03%) and most efficient hemicellulose (97.02%) and lignin removal (70.89%). The removal of amorphous lignin enhanced the crystallinity of the residues and improved the conversion efficiency of cellulose into levulinic acid. Additionally, the structural alterations in lignin samples were analyzed in comparison to milled wood lignin (MWL). The PEG200-OA system facilitated the cleavage of β-O-4 and β-5 linkages and resulted in the degradation of S-type lignin, accompanied by increased condensation of G units. The resulting lignin displayed a reduced molecular weight (Mw of 1283 g/mol, Mn value 531 g/mol) and nanoscale particle size (D50 212 nm). Furthermore, fluorescent lignin was synthesized through simple oxidation and was used to detect metal ions. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations supported that both PEG200 and OA played a significant role in lignin dissolution, with the weak interactions between DES and lignin primarily driven by hydrogen bonding (characterized as weak, closed-shell, and electrostatic) and van der Waals forces. ## 1. Introduction As global fossil fuel reserves dwindle and environmental challenges intensify, the role of bio-refinery technology in efficiently converting lignocellulosic biomass into energy and chemicals becomes increasingly important. Lignocellulose primarily consists of hemicellulose (23% to 32%), cellulose (38% to 50%), and lignin (15% to 25%) [1]. Hemi-cellulose and cellulose can be hydrolyzed or pyrolyzed to produce various biofuels and biochemicals, including monosaccharides like mannose, glucose, and arabinose [2,3]. Lignin, a complex and amorphous polymer, is derived from phenylpropane units and features a variety of hydrophilic functional groups such as carboxylic acids and hydroxyl groups [4]. This unique structure allows lignin to be used in the production of lignin-based nanoparticles, flocculants, and luminescent materials, among other applications [5-7]. However, the intricate network of covalent and hydrogen bonds linking cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin poses significant challenges for biomass utilization [8]. Pretreatment of lignocellulose is a crucial step in improving its usability and sustainability [9]. This process alters the biomass's structural com- ponents, making it more amenable to conversion into valuable products while reducing waste and meeting the growing demand for high-value commodities [9]. Various pretreatment methods, such as alkaline treatments and organic solvent applications, have been developed to enhance this transformation [10]. However, traditional pretreatment methods often face significant challenges, including equipment corrosion, volatility issues, and the requirement for extreme conditions, all of which pose operational risks and can diminish profitability [11]. Additionally, during many pretreatment processes, lignin is prone to depolymerization and condensation, complicating its recovery and subsequent use. Therefore, the development of more efficient and environmentally friendly pretreatment strategies is crucial for optimizing the economic and ecological benefits of lignocellulose utilization [11]. Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) are gaining great attention as prom- ising, eco-friendly alternatives to traditional solvents for the fraction- ation of biomass components [12,13]. International Journal of Biological Macromolecules 297 (2025) 139922 non-toxicity, and low volatility, DESs are typically formed by combining two or more components that create a eutectic mixture with a melting point lower than that of the individual components [14]. The formation of a network of hydrogen bonds between a hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA) and a hydrogen bond donor (HBD) enhances the dissolution and separation of biomass components [14]. In the pretreatment of ligno-cellulosic biomass, DESs have shown a remarkable ability to disrupt the lignin-carbohydrate complex (LCC) and improve lignin dissolution [13,15,16]. This effectiveness has led to the exploration of various DES formulations to overcome biomass recalcitrance in bioenergy production. Additionally, reactive DESs offer the advantage of introducing functional groups such as carbonyl, carboxylic, and ammonium groups during pretreatment [15]. This dual functionality can reduce the need for additional chemicals and energy inputs, presenting a more sustain-able approach to biomass conversion. China is the world's largest producer and consumer of tea. The deep processing of tea into products like tea beverages, instant tea, and tea polyphenols generates substantial amounts of tea stem [17,18]. Disposing of this residue as waste not only squanders valuable resources but also poses environmental risks, contributing to pollution and ecological damage. Tea stem is primarily composed of cellulose, hemi-cellulose and lignin. Currently, the focus of tea stem utilization in China is largely on extracting active compounds such as tea polyphenols and tea polysaccharides [19]. However, the potential value-added applica-tions of lignin, hemicellulose, and cellulose from tea stem remain largely underexplored. Therefore, pretreating tea stem to effectively separate cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin is crucial for the sustainable utili-zation of tea stem resources, offering significant environmental and economic benefits. DESs have been used for the pretreatment of multiple lignocelluloses [20,21], however, there remains a significant opportu-nity to derive greater value from the extracted fractions of tea stem. Besides, beyond the conversion of carbohydrates into biofuels and bio-chemicals, further utilization of lignin could enhance both the economic viability and environmental sustainability of lignocellulose-based bio-refineries [20,21]. In our study, we present a novel approach for converting tea stem into high-value products. We utilized PDESs composed of PEG200 and OA as an innovative reactive medium for breaking down tea stem, enabling the selective separation of lignocellulosic components. PEG200 serves as a hydrogen bond acceptor and is known for its low viscosity and ability to dissolve a wide range of biomass components, making it an ideal candidate for biomass pretreatment. Organic acids, such as oxalic acid, are efficient hydrogen bond donors, which facilitate the formation of stable DES with PEG200. This specific combination has been shown to enhance the solubility and disrupt the structural integrity of lignocel- lulosic materials, promoting better pretreatment efficiency. Through various analytical techniques, we assessed the impact of PDES treatment on the biomass structure, confirming its effectiveness in selective delignification and hemicellulose removal. We further enhanced the value of the cellulosic fraction by converting it into levulinic acid (LA), one of the top ten pivotal platform chemicals identified by the U.S. Department of Energy, thus maximizing the utility of cellulose derived from tea stem [22]. This conversion process not only increased the economic potential of the biomass but also confirmed the pretreatment method enhanced cellulose digestibility. The recovered lignin was thoroughly characterized, including analyses of molecular weight, par- ticle size, and structural properties, with comparisons drawn to milled wood lignin (MWL) to underscore the unique attributes resulting from our process. Moreover, the application of the recovered lignin was explored by synthesizing fluorescent lignin via a simple method, which was successfully utilized in detecting Fe3+ ions, opening new possibil- ities for lignin use. Furthermore, density functional theory (DFT) cal- culations were employed, with the combination of the experimental results to provide a comprehensive understanding of the mechanisms driving efficient lignin extraction. Overall, this study introduced the PDES system composed of PEG200 and oxalic acid for efficiently breaking down tea stem, enabling selective lignocellulose separation and high-value conversion of cellulose into levulinic acid. Additionally, the recovered lignin was valorized as a fluorescent material for Fe3+ detection, and DFT analysis provided new insights into the extraction mechanisms, showcasing a sustainable and integrated approach for agricultural byproduct utilization. ## 2. Materials and methods ### 2.1. Materials Tea stem, obtained from a local vendor in Xiamen, China, were first rinsed with deionized water and then subjected to thermal drying at 80 °C to eliminate moisture. After drying, the material was mechanically ground and passed through an 80-mesh sieve to produce a consistent, fine tea stem powder. This powder was directly used in subsequent experiments without further modification. PEG200 was purchased from Aladdin Reagent Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China. Various organic acids, including levulinic acid, oxalic acid, formic acid, and lactic acid, were sourced from Rhawn Reagent Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China. Additionally, the catalyst 1-sulfobutyl-3-methylimidazole p-toluenesulfonate ([C4SO3Hmim][PhSO3]), with a purity of over 99%, was supplied by Shanghai Cheng Jie Chemical Co., Ltd. Other analytical-grade chemicals were procured from Aladdin Reagent Co., Ltd. 2.2. Preparation of deep eutectic solvent The selected organic acids and PEG200 were mixed in 1:2 M ratio and blended under vigorous stirring at 80 °C, resulting in the formation of translucent DES. After cooling to room temperature, the solution remained clear and uniform, confirming the successful synthesis of the DESs. Using a similar approach, a series of PEG200-OA DESs, varying the molar ratios of HBA/HBD, was prepared. 2.3. The results indicated that PEG200-based Brønsted acid PDESs were effective in delignifying tea stem, achieving successful removal of lignin and hemicellulose. Besides, PEG200, as a hydrogen bond donor, has low viscosity and excellent solvent properties, allowing it to effectively dissolve various biomass components. Oxalic acid, serving as a hydrogen bond acceptor, helps to form a stable DES with PEG200, enhancing the solubility of lignocellulosic materials. This combination could disrupt the structural integrity of lignocellulose by weakening hydrogen bonds, facilitating the selective separation of lignin and hemicellulose. Consequently, PEG200-OA was selected as the optimal DES for subsequent experiments. Lignin, an amorphous polymer composed of methoxylated phenyl-propane units linked with phenolic groups [33], was known for emitting strong fluorescence across the visible and far-infrared spectra [34]. To investigate this, fluorescence microscopy was employed to monitor lignin's dissolution dynamics in the different PDES systems, as depicted in Fig. 1B. Initially, intense fluorescence was observed in the tea stem solids, with no fluorescence detected in the solvent phase, indicating that lignin was densely encapsulating the tea stem solids. As the disso-lution progressed in the various PDES systems, fluorescence began to appear in the solution, demonstrating effective lignin removal. The PEG200-OA system exhibited significantly higher fluorescence intensity in the solution compared to other systems, indicating greater lignin extraction. Utilization of the cellulose-rich solid residues Extensive research had been dedicated to transforming biomass into valuable intermediates, with particular emphasis on LA due to its versatility and potential applications. As lignin is a highly recalcitrant polymer, its presence in the biomass matrix significantly hinders the accessibility of cellulose to catalytic action, thus reducing the efficiency of cellulose conversion. Lignin removal helps to disrupt the biomass structure, improving the porosity and accessibility of cellulose, which in turn enhances its conversion to levulinic acid. In this study, we effec- tively removed lignin during the pretreatment process. As illustrated in Fig. 3B, LA production markedly increased from 35.7% to 51.5% following PEG200-OA pretreatment. Thus, pretreating tea stem with PEG200-OA significantly enhanced the conversion of cellulose into LA, optimizing the overall process. Therefore, the PEG200-OA pretreatment successfully removed lignin and hemicellulose without compromising the integrity of the cellulose structure. Calculation and analysis of intermolecular interaction by DFT In the previous section, the PEG200-OA PDES system demonstrated considerable effectiveness in lignocellulose pretreatment, particularly in its ability to dissolve lignin. This effectiveness was closely related to the interaction between the PDES components and lignin. To better understand the mechanisms underlying lignin dissolution, we conducted DFT calculations to analyze the interactions between the PEG200-OA system and lignin [51,52]. The geometries of the interaction complexes between PEG200-OA and p-coumaryl alcohol, coniferyl alcohol, and sinapyl alcohol were optimized, with the most stable structures shown in Fig. 7. 2- Fig. 7 illustrated the weak intermolecular interactions identified using the RDG function isosurface (top) and scatter diagram (bottom). Based on the Sign (λ²)p values, these interactions were categorized into hydrogen bonds (blue), van der Waals forces (green), and steric effects (red) [31]. Our analysis revealed that hydrogen bonds and van der Waals forces were the primary interactions between PEG200-OA and lignin, with both the HBA and HBD playing a synergistic role in lignin removal. Notably, the hydrogen bonds in the PEG200-OA-lignin com- plex were formed between the hydrogen atom on the carboxyl group of the HBD (OA) and the oxygen atom on the alkyl hydroxyl group of lignin. The properties of these hydrogen bonds were further elucidated through topological analysis using AIM theory, as summarized in Fig. 7. It was found that the ρ at the BCP of a hydrogen bond typically ranged from 0.002 to 0.035 au, while the ∇²ρ at the BCP of non-covalent in- teractions, such as hydrogen bonds, generally fell within the range of 0.024 to 0.139 au. The values of ρ and ∇²ρ for the hydrogen bonds between PEG200 and OA fell within these ranges, confirming the for- mation of hydrogen bonds. According to established theories [32,53], the strength and nature of hydrogen bonds can be determined by specific criteria. If both the ∇²ρ and the H were negative, the hydrogen bond is considered strong, shared, and covalently dominant. Conversely, if ∇²ρ was positive and H was negative, the bond was of medium strength, closed-shell, and covalently dominant. In cases where both ∇²ρ and H are positive, the hydrogen bond was classified as weak, closed-shell, and electrostatic dominant. In our study, the positive values of ∇²ρ and H indicated that the interactions between PEG200-OA and lignin were weak, closed-shell, and electrostatic in nature. 4. Specially, combining PEG200 and oxalic acid (OA) exhibited a notably high cellulose retention (82.03%) and most efficient hemicellulose (97.02%) and lignin removal (70.89%). The removal of amorphous lignin enhanced the crystallinity of the residues and improved the conversion efficiency of cellulose into levulinic acid. Additionally, the structural alterations in lignin samples were analyzed in comparison to milled wood lignin (MWL). The PEG200-OA system facilitated the cleavage of β-O-4 and β-5 linkages and resulted in the degradation of S-type lignin, accompanied by increased condensation of G units. The resulting lignin displayed a reduced molecular weight (Mw of 1283 g/mol, Mn value 531 g/mol) and nanoscale particle size (D50 212 nm). Furthermore, fluorescent lignin was synthesized through simple oxidation and was used to detect metal ions. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations supported that both PEG200 and OA played a significant role in lignin dissolution, with the weak interactions between DES and lignin primarily driven by hydrogen bonding (characterized as weak, closed-shell, and electrostatic) and van der Waals forces. ## 1. Introduction As global fossil fuel reserves dwindle and environmental challenges intensify, the role of bio-refinery technology in efficiently converting lignocellulosic biomass into energy and chemicals becomes increasingly important. Lignocellulose primarily consists of hemicellulose (23% to 32%), cellulose (38% to 50%), and lignin (15% to 25%) [1]. Hemi-cellulose and cellulose can be hydrolyzed or pyrolyzed to produce various biofuels and biochemicals, including monosaccharides like mannose, glucose, and arabinose [2,3]. Lignin, a complex and amorphous polymer, is derived from phenylpropane units and features a variety of hydrophilic functional groups such as carboxylic acids and hydroxyl groups [4]. This unique structure allows lignin to be used in the production of lignin-based nanoparticles, flocculants, and luminescent materials, among other applications [5-7]. However, the intricate network of covalent and hydrogen bonds linking cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin poses significant challenges for biomass utilization [8]. Pretreatment of lignocellulose is a crucial step in improving its usability and sustainability [9]. This process alters the biomass's structural com- ponents, making it more amenable to conversion into valuable products while reducing waste and meeting the growing demand for high-value commodities [9]. Various pretreatment methods, such as alkaline treatments and organic solvent applications, have been developed to enhance this transformation [10]. However, traditional pretreatment methods often face significant challenges, including equipment corrosion, volatility issues, and the requirement for extreme conditions, all of which pose operational risks and can diminish profitability [11]. Additionally, during many pretreatment processes, lignin is prone to depolymerization and condensation, complicating its recovery and subsequent use. Therefore, the development of more efficient and environmentally friendly pretreatment strategies is crucial for optimizing the economic and ecological benefits of lignocellulose utilization [11]. Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) are gaining great attention as prom- ising, eco-friendly alternatives to traditional solvents for the fraction- ation of biomass components [12,13]. The formation of a network of hydrogen bonds between a hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA) and a hydrogen bond donor (HBD) enhances the dissolution and separation of biomass components [14]. In the pretreatment of ligno-cellulosic biomass, DESs have shown a remarkable ability to disrupt the lignin-carbohydrate complex (LCC) and improve lignin dissolution [13,15,16]. This effectiveness has led to the exploration of various DES formulations to overcome biomass recalcitrance in bioenergy production. Additionally, reactive DESs offer the advantage of introducing functional groups such as carbonyl, carboxylic, and ammonium groups during pretreatment [15]. This dual functionality can reduce the need for additional chemicals and energy inputs, presenting a more sustain-able approach to biomass conversion. China is the world's largest producer and consumer of tea. The deep processing of tea into products like tea beverages, instant tea, and tea polyphenols generates substantial amounts of tea stem [17,18]. Disposing of this residue as waste not only squanders valuable resources but also poses environmental risks, contributing to pollution and ecological damage. Tea stem is primarily composed of cellulose, hemi-cellulose and lignin. Currently, the focus of tea stem utilization in China is largely on extracting active compounds such as tea polyphenols and tea polysaccharides [19]. However, the potential value-added applica-tions of lignin, hemicellulose, and cellulose from tea stem remain largely underexplored. Therefore, pretreating tea stem to effectively separate cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin is crucial for the sustainable utili-zation of tea stem resources, offering significant environmental and economic benefits. DESs have been used for the pretreatment of multiple lignocelluloses [20,21], however, there remains a significant opportu-nity to derive greater value from the extracted fractions of tea stem. Besides, beyond the conversion of carbohydrates into biofuels and bio-chemicals, further utilization of lignin could enhance both the economic viability and environmental sustainability of lignocellulose-based bio-refineries [20,21]. In our study, we present a novel approach for converting tea stem into high-value products. We utilized PDESs composed of PEG200 and OA as an innovative reactive medium for breaking down tea stem, enabling the selective separation of lignocellulosic components. PEG200 serves as a hydrogen bond acceptor and is known for its low viscosity and ability to dissolve a wide range of biomass components, making it an ideal candidate for biomass pretreatment. Organic acids, such as oxalic acid, are efficient hydrogen bond donors, which facilitate the formation of stable DES with PEG200. This specific combination has been shown to enhance the solubility and disrupt the structural integrity of lignocel- lulosic materials, promoting better pretreatment efficiency. Through various analytical techniques, we assessed the impact of PDES treatment on the biomass structure, confirming its effectiveness in selective delignification and hemicellulose removal. We further enhanced the value of the cellulosic fraction by converting it into levulinic acid (LA), one of the top ten pivotal platform chemicals identified by the U.S. Department of Energy, thus maximizing the utility of cellulose derived from tea stem [22]. This conversion process not only increased the economic potential of the biomass but also confirmed the pretreatment method enhanced cellulose digestibility. The recovered lignin was thoroughly characterized, including analyses of molecular weight, par- ticle size, and structural properties, with comparisons drawn to milled wood lignin (MWL) to underscore the unique attributes resulting from our process. Moreover, the application of the recovered lignin was explored by synthesizing fluorescent lignin via a simple method, which was successfully utilized in detecting Fe3+ ions, opening new possibil- ities for lignin use. Furthermore, density functional theory (DFT) cal- culations were employed, with the combination of the experimental results to provide a comprehensive understanding of the mechanisms driving efficient lignin extraction. Overall, this study introduced the PDES system composed of PEG200 and oxalic acid for efficiently breaking down tea stem, enabling selective lignocellulose separation and high-value conversion of cellulose into levulinic acid. Additionally, the recovered lignin was valorized as a fluorescent material for Fe3+ detection, and DFT analysis provided new insights into the extraction mechanisms, showcasing a sustainable and integrated approach for agricultural byproduct utilization. ## 2. Materials and methods ### 2.1. Materials Tea stem, obtained from a local vendor in Xiamen, China, were first rinsed with deionized water and then subjected to thermal drying at 80 °C to eliminate moisture. After drying, the material was mechanically ground and passed through an 80-mesh sieve to produce a consistent, fine tea stem powder. This powder was directly used in subsequent experiments without further modification. PEG200 was purchased from Aladdin Reagent Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China. Various organic acids, including levulinic acid, oxalic acid, formic acid, and lactic acid, were sourced from Rhawn Reagent Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China. As lignin is a highly recalcitrant polymer, its presence in the biomass matrix significantly hinders the accessibility of cellulose to catalytic action, thus reducing the efficiency of cellulose conversion. Calculation and analysis of intermolecular interaction by DFT In the previous section, the PEG200-OA PDES system demonstrated considerable effectiveness in lignocellulose pretreatment, particularly in its ability to dissolve lignin. This effectiveness was closely related to the interaction between the PDES components and lignin. To better understand the mechanisms underlying lignin dissolution, we conducted DFT calculations to analyze the interactions between the PEG200-OA system and lignin [51,52]. The geometries of the interaction complexes between PEG200-OA and p-coumaryl alcohol, coniferyl alcohol, and sinapyl alcohol were optimized, with the most stable structures shown in Fig. 7. 2- Fig. 7 illustrated the weak intermolecular interactions identified using the RDG function isosurface (top) and scatter diagram (bottom). Based on the Sign (λ²)p values, these interactions were categorized into hydrogen bonds (blue), van der Waals forces (green), and steric effects (red) [31]. Our analysis revealed that hydrogen bonds and van der Waals forces were the primary interactions between PEG200-OA and lignin, with both the HBA and HBD playing a synergistic role in lignin removal. Notably, the hydrogen bonds in the PEG200-OA-lignin com- plex were formed between the hydrogen atom on the carboxyl group of the HBD (OA) and the oxygen atom on the alkyl hydroxyl group of lignin. The properties of these hydrogen bonds were further elucidated through topological analysis using AIM theory, as summarized in Fig. 7. It was found that the ρ at the BCP of a hydrogen bond typically ranged from 0.002 to 0.035 au, while the ∇²ρ at the BCP of non-covalent in- teractions, such as hydrogen bonds, generally fell within the range of 0.024 to 0.139 au. The values of ρ and ∇²ρ for the hydrogen bonds between PEG200 and OA fell within these ranges, confirming the for- mation of hydrogen bonds. According to established theories [32,53], the strength and nature of hydrogen bonds can be determined by specific criteria. If both the ∇²ρ and the H were negative, the hydrogen bond is considered strong, shared, and covalently dominant. Conversely, if ∇²ρ was positive and H was negative, the bond was of medium strength, closed-shell, and covalently dominant. In cases where both ∇²ρ and H are positive, the hydrogen bond was classified as weak, closed-shell, and electrostatic dominant. In our study, the positive values of ∇²ρ and H indicated that the interactions between PEG200-OA and lignin were weak, closed-shell, and electrostatic in nature. 4.
